overview:
What Americans call the Vietnam War and Vietnamese call the Resistance War Against America began as the unfinished business of French decolonization. The 1954 Geneva agreements ended French rule and split the country at the 17th parallel, pending elections that were never held; by 1955 Ngo Dinh Diem had consolidated a US-backed state in the south and Ho Chi Minh's Democratic Republic of Vietnam governed the north. Through the late 1950s the conflict was mostly a southern insurgency — communist cadres, land disputes, village-level assassination and reprisal — fought by South Vietnamese troops with American advisers. The 1963 battle of Ap Bac, where a much larger government force was mauled by a smaller Viet Cong unit, exposed how badly that arrangement was working. After the reported attacks on US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin in August 1964, Congress passed a resolution that became the legal basis on which Johnson and then Nixon prosecuted the war; sustained bombing of the north followed in 1965, and American ground troops arrived in force. The Ia Drang valley that November was the first large set-piece battle between US and North Vietnamese regulars, and it set the pattern of the years that followed: search-and-destroy operations, body counts, and an enemy that could absorb losses and choose when to fight.

The war never stayed inside Vietnam. Supply moved south along the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia, and American bombing followed it, eventually dropping more ordnance on those two countries than on Vietnam itself and helping destabilize Cambodia toward the Khmer Rouge. Allied contingents fought too — South Korean divisions, and the Australians and New Zealanders whose stand at Long Tan in 1966 became their defining engagement of the war. The turning point was political rather than military. The Tet Offensive of early 1968 was a battlefield defeat for the communist forces, who lost enormous numbers of fighters and failed to trigger a general uprising, but the month-long house-to-house destruction of Hue and the sight of fighting inside the US embassy compound in Saigon broke American confidence that the war was being won. The siege of Khe Sanh ran alongside it. In March of the same year an American company killed several hundred unarmed villagers at My Lai; the massacre stayed hidden for over a year, and its exposure, together with costly assaults like Hamburger Hill in 1969, hardened opposition at home.

Nixon's answer was Vietnamization — withdrawing American troops while expanding air power and arming Saigon — alongside secret negotiations that produced the Paris Peace Accords in January 1973. The accords got the last US combat forces out and the American prisoners home, but left North Vietnamese divisions in place in the south and settled nothing. When Hanoi launched its final offensive in spring 1975, South Vietnamese resistance collapsed in weeks; helicopters lifted the last evacuees off Saigon rooftops on 30 April. Cambodia fell to the Khmer Rouge the same month, and the Mayaguez incident that May — a bungled US rescue operation off the Cambodian coast — became the last American combat deaths of the era. Estimates of the dead vary enormously and are genuinely contested: something between one and three million Vietnamese, roughly half or more of them civilians, plus hundreds of thousands in Cambodia and Laos and 58,000 Americans.
significance: The war ended the assumption, held in Washington since 1945, that overwhelming industrial firepower could reliably impose political outcomes on a determined nationalist movement, and it did so in front of television cameras. Domestically it produced a rupture in American public trust — over the Tonkin incident, over My Lai, over the Pentagon Papers — whose language and reflexes still shape how Western publics argue about foreign wars, and it drove concrete constraints like the War Powers Resolution and the end of conscription. For Vietnam it delivered unification at a staggering cost, followed by a decade of isolation, boat-people emigration, and the lasting damage of unexploded ordnance and dioxin defoliants. Regionally its worst consequence fell on Cambodia, where the bombing and the collapse of order helped open the way to genocide. The war also reshaped the Cold War itself, exposing the Sino-Soviet split as Hanoi maneuvered between its two patrons and making the limits of superpower proxy conflict visible to everyone watching.
coverage: Written from the general reference accounts below plus a survey of casualty estimates, which differ by a factor of three depending on method and source — no figure here should be read as settled. The dataset's 75 events skew heavily toward named battles involving American and allied troops, which mirrors a documentary record that is vastly richer on the US side: Party and military archives in Hanoi remain largely closed, so North Vietnamese and NLF decision-making is reconstructed from a thin and selectively released base, and the experience of South Vietnamese civilians and soldiers is thinner still. The air war over Laos and Cambodia, the Republic of Vietnam's own politics, and the postwar reeducation camps and refugee exodus are barely represented in the events beneath this story.
